utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start, the Chamber would like to deliver a decision; that is, the decision on the Prosecution's 10th motion for testimony via video-conference link. On the 29th of October, 2007, the Prosecution filed its motion for testimony via video-conference link and for trial-related protective measures for a witness who, until then, had been the subject of a Rule 92 bis application. The application for protective measures will be the subject of a separate decision by the Chamber. As the decision on this has not yet been taken, the Chamber will not refer to the witness by name. As for the video-conference link, the Prosecution argues that the witness is of advanced age and has health problems, including a weak heart. The witness states that exposure to stress would be dangerous for him and that his age and health condition do not allow him to travel long distances. The Defence does not oppose the application. While the Prosecution has not provided any medical documentation in support of its application, the Chamber finds that, based on the information provided, a journey to The Hague to give testimony would involve discomfort and health risks for the witness. It also finds the expected testimony to be sufficiently important and the mode of delivery of the testimony to be compatible with the accused's right to confront the witness. The Chamber therefore finds that it is in the interests of justice to hear the witness via video-conference link. The motion is therefore granted. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder if I just might briefly before the next witness is brought in raise one or two matters which have previously been raised and during the course of procedural argument just prior to the time when the witness was last due to be called. There is, as I understand it, no application for protective measures in respect of this witness, and so I shall use his name. His name is Pjeter Shala, and as Your Honours know, he is named in the indictment as a member, alleged, of the joint criminal enterprise that the Prosecution alleges here. So as, in effect, to bring him within alleged responsibility for all crimes alleged on the indictment, as well as specific allegations of participation, which he in suspect interviews in the past has denied. The position as we understand it is as follows: The Prosecution currently contends that Mr. Shala directly participated in two crimes alleged on the indictment; that is to say -- or two pairs of crimes; that is to say, counts 33 and 34, the alleged abduction of (redacted) and another, and one of the sub-counts in count 22, the alleged abduction and murder of Zdravko Radunovic, both of which, as I indicated a moment ago, the witness denied in suspect interviews conducted first in 2005 and then by Mr. Di Fazio as a suspect interview in 2007, in May of this year. I raised a number of issues arising out of this slightly unusual situation in argument at an earlier stage, and I have, purely for convenience, provided the Chamber with a paper copy of an extract from the transcript. The first question which arises is the question of caution in respect of a witness who is being called by the Prosecution when it is alleged that he's a member of the JCE and indeed when he denies the allegations that the Prosecution contend he is responsible for. And if I could just briefly remind the Trial Chamber of the position that was then thought to be appropriate, at page 4585, line 4 of the transcript. If I could, without -- I think -- I think -- do I understand the Trial Chamber has a copy of the document in front? And simply the -- the first and second sentence is in the remarks listed at line 4 by Your Honour, Judge Orie. Now, the position is, as I indicated a moment ago, not only was Mr. Shala treated as a suspect in 2005 but this is not a situation where, to use Your Honour's words, the suspicion has been clearly removed, because, as I indicated in 2007, the suspect interview provisions and caution were administered in relation to him by Mr. Di Fazio as well, and it remains the Prosecution case that despite his denials he is responsible for those alleged crimes. So that -- that's the first issue that I wanted to raise. The second relates to what the appropriate content of the caution should be, and in particular, whether or not it is clear and has been clear to this witness what it is that's alleged against him. I raise this at page 4588 of the transcript, where I sought further and better particulars of the indictment and pre-trial brief and specifically a request for clarification of exactly what it was that then - that is, the 22nd of May - the Prosecution were alleging Mr. Shala's participation to be. And that application was resolved by agreement with Mr. Re kindly agreeing to provide that information in writing by letter. The letter that he wrote on the same day is at tab 22 -- I'm sorry, is at tab 2 of the bundle and indicates that the allegations against Mr. Shala referred to counts 33 and 34, and in support of that, to paragraphs 27 and 107 of the revised second amended indictment and paragraphs 32 to 34 and 151 of the pre-trial brief. Each of those citations relates to counts 33 and 34, the alleged abduction of (redacted) (redacted); in other words, there was no mention in that letter of the allegation of murder, perhaps one might think the more serious of the two, that is made by the Prosecution in respect of Zdravko Radunovic in counts 21 and 22. Seeing that, I wrote to Mr. Re the following day in the terms of the e-mail at tab 3 of the bundle. And as far as relevance, it is the second paragraph of that letter that is of significance, where I communicate my reading of that letter from Mr. Re as an indication that the passages referred to represent the entirety of the criminal conduct alleged against Mr. Shala and seeking immediate correction if that assumption were wrong, and no correction was given. So in those circumstances, it would appear that as at the 22nd of May, the position taken by the Prosecution was that Mr. Shala was, despite his denials, guilty of the allegation in counts 33 and 34, but that it was not then being contended that he was guilty of the murder alleged in counts 21 and 22. That is, as we understand it now, being alleged by the Prosecution. And in our submission, that certainly raises an issue for the Trial Chamber to consider as regards, first of all, the content of the caution; and secondly, the question of whether or not the effect of the caution needs to be explained to Mr. Shala by independent legal advice. I say that because, as I understand it, the way the Prosecution proposes to deal with this witness is not to elicit from him the testimony that consists of denials to the specific allegations that are made. Now, of course, there are two -- two dimensions to that. The first is that in any event the allegation against him is of all counts in the indictment as a member of a joint criminal enterprise; and secondly, that the Prosecution does, for example, just by way of illustration, propose to elicit from this witness his presence at the time and place of the alleged abduction of Zdravko Radunovic. So the fact that Mr. Di Fazio takes the position that he won't seek to ask specific questions in order to elicit the witness's denial to the particular acts of participation that the Prosecution now alleges against him, in our submission, doesn't obviate the need for consideration, and both of caution and of the position that the witness may find himself in answering questions without the nature of the allegations the Prosecution makes being properly explained to him and having had the opportunity to take advice in respect of it. So I thought it only right, given the fact that the matter has been raised already on the transcript, to return to it and put those matters before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join in the submissions. I have nothing further to add at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I take the same position, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you need to respond? MR. DI FAZIO: It's not entirely clear to me what the Defence are inviting you to do. It seems to be that they would like you to provide or give the witness an opportunity to take legal advice, and I gather that they would like you to provide the witness with a caution - perhaps if I may phrase it in this way, in general terms - before he testifies. My submission is that under the Rules, in particular, Rule 90(E), you should not administer any caution as and up until the point in his testimony where he starts to say something that may incriminate him. There's just no call for it up until that point. And therefore, that's the way the Prosecution -- the Prosecution would invite you to -- to deal with this particular issue. The -- Mr. Emmerson is right in the sense that I don't propose to put questions to the witness about those specific incidents in those counts, the counts relating to the witness who was abducted and the other count relating to the Serbian policeman. I don't think that precludes me from asking the witness questions about his location and what he was doing at the time of either of those incidents without a caution being administered. It's only if I ask him questions that might invite an answer indicating direct involvement or involvement in those particular crimes that the -- the question of a -- of a -- of a caution might arise. The Rule 90(E) says: "A witness may object to the making of a statement which might tend to incriminate him" and that you can then compel the witness to answer that question -- that question and that the testimony compelled in that way can't be used against him. It calls for no general warning or administration of a caution prior to the witness testifying or a warning to be given at the beginning of his testimony so that the witness himself doesn't stumble into the making of any particular incriminating -- self-incriminating statement. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber is in a good position to be able to observe that the rights that accrue to the witness under 90(E), are well observed because you know the facts in this case and you know if he was going be led into an area where he -- he might reasonably expect to want to object himself to answering the question. So, essentially, the position is you should not administer a caution up until the time that it's clearly called for and up until the time that the witness is being invited to say something which may in fact incriminate him. Until he says -- until he covers the material in those two particular counts, it's the Prosecution's submission that that won't occur, won't give rise to that necessity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, if I may. First of all, what is unusual about the position of this individual, as opposed to witnesses in general, is his position as a named member of the JCE. Secondly, the issue of what may tend to incriminate in the context of an allegation of membership of the JCE, is, in our submission, not something which is easily discernible by the witness without knowing exactly what it is that's alleged against him. And being in a position to consider his position with advice. But I -- I made the submissions that we wish to make and put before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I only have one brief addition, which is: What is the harm in -- in cautioning the man when he's in as delicate a legal position as he is? MR. DI FAZIO: If I may just answer that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. MR. DI FAZIO: -- point. The suggestion that he's in a delicate legal position is, in the Prosecution's submission, not strictly correct. As we said, it's -- it's going to be easily identifiable for you to -- to -- to see when he's -- if I were to stray into an area that might give rise to self-incriminating statements. So it's not -- not a delicate position. And the harm is that it's going to cause the -- the witness considerable concern and apprehension and may take -- colour the manner which he gives evidence. He should be able to testify as freely as he can. And if he reaches the point where he is being led into making self-incriminatory statements, then -- then and only then, the protections that arise under 90(E) should activate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One additional question to both parties: Does it play any role that the time to bring any new indictments against persons has expired and that therefore there's no risk of further being prosecuted before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: One is in a rather odd position, because obviously we don't represent Mr. Shala and so one is having to put oneself into the position, so to speak, of the hypothetical lawyer advising him. But in our submission the answer to that question would be no, because plainly were he to be examined by Mr. Di Fazio to put himself in a position where he was both present at the time and place of the commission allegedly of a particular crime in the testimony that he gives in this court, then in the absence of greater examination legally as to the position, there would appear to be no bar to that testimony being used as the basis for prosecution in another jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, Mr. Guy-Smith, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not only prosecution but any other collateral proceedings that may directly affect him, such as representations with regard to asylum applications or refugee applications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Agreed. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But one question, then: Is the right to remain silent, is that given in order to protect the witness in his civil or administrative dealings elsewhere, or is that the purpose of -- the right to remain silent --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a general proposition obviously it's not. What we're dealing with is the privilege against self-incrimination and compelled testimony in the absence of knowing an intelligent waiver there of. I think the difficulty is -- and really as has been defined already by Mr. Emmerson, is that you have a gentleman who's in a situation who has potential criminal liability, whether it be in this Tribunal or it be somewhere else, because the kinds of crimes that are being discussed are crimes that could be prosecuted in other jurisdictions. And quite frankly, I think for purposes of -- of -- really -- and once again, he's -- as Mr. Emmerson's saying - and I say the same thing - he's not my client, but with regard to the protection of any individual and the integrity of the proceedings, I think it's pretty important that a witness situated as he is, at least has some understanding of what the potential of his testimony could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, any need? MR. DI FAZIO: Just -- just to say this, if Your Honours please: In reply to the question of does the fact of this institution or proceeding with other indictments affect the operation of Rule 90(E), without taking instructions and without an opportunity to research the matter, it would not be appropriate for me to comment upon that, and I decline to do so. I -- all I can say -- all I can do is -- just another observation is that the right to silence is somewhat mitigated in that Rule because it says that testimony is compellable -- you can compel the witness to answer. So it's not an absolute right. It appears not to be an absolute right. It's just that such testimony can't be used against him in -- in subsequent prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will withdraw, likely very limited -- a very limited time, to discuss how to proceed. The parties are expected to remain on stand-by. --- Break taken at 2.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, do you consider the witness to be called, Pjeter Shala, still to be a suspect for the purposes of the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If he was to be interviewed again, he would -- the Rules would kick in; he would be interviewed as a suspect. And that's what happened in -- earlier this year, when I conducted an interview with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To interview someone as a suspect, doesn't that mean that you do that in order to prepare possible prosecution of that person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: The Rules, if Your Honours please, have a regime that deal with the situation, and they contain -- they have a definition of -- of "suspect" which covers the situation of Mr. Shala. I'm just trying to find it -- I was just trying to find it, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please find it. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm looking at -- I think we find it in Rules -- around Rule 39. If Your Honours would just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, Rule 42 deals with the interview of a suspect. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that's right. It contains the -- the definition -- that's right. The Rules also contain a definition of "suspect," if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that 2 or -- yes. MR. DI FAZIO: 2. Rule 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "The person concerning whom the Prosecutor possesses reliable information which tends to show that the person may have committed a crime over which the Tribunal has jurisdiction." MR. DI FAZIO: May have committed. It's, if I may say so, couched in broad terms. It's information -- reliable information which tends to show that he may have committed a crime. And it's -- it's a broad definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: He is, of course, not a target of any -- of any investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? MR. DI FAZIO: He is not a target of any investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's not a target of any investigation at this moment, so, theoretically, you would say he's a suspect but he's not at this moment -- MR. DI FAZIO: He falls within that definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- MR. DI FAZIO: Theoretically or otherwise, he falls within that definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that any -- any -- bringing an indictment against him is considered to be totally impossible in the present stages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I can safely indicate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided that it will not caution the witness at the beginning of his testimony. At the same time, the Chamber will start the examination of the witness by verifying a few matters and informing him about a few matters as well. Therefore, Mr. Di Fazio, I do understand that there's no application for protective measures? MR. DI FAZIO: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may call your next witness, being Mr. Pjeter Shala, if I'm well informed. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness, can we just briefly go into private -- private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: It's only a very brief matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do so -- before we do so, Mr. Di Fazio, when I said that I'll not give a caution to the witness in the beginning of his testimony, that does not exclude for the possibility that the Chamber would consider at a certain moment that there is a need to do so. That will depend on the course of the examination and -- MR. DI FAZIO: Entirely. Entirely. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's now just for the parties to be informed about this. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you'd like to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Shala. Can you hear me in a language you understand? Before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shala, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shala, before the examination starts, the Chamber would like to know whether you are aware that your name appear in -- appears in the indictment which was brought against the accused. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber further would like to inform you that although you have been interviewed as a suspect and that you still officially qualify as a suspect, that is, someone who -- of whom there are reasons to believe that you may have committed a crime, that at this moment you are not the target of any investigation by this Tribunal at this moment and that you cannot be prosecuted any more before this Tribunal. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I'm learning that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, further the Chamber would like to know whether you are aware of -- of any investigation or any case which we -- will be brought against you, any prosecution in any other jurisdiction. The Chamber has no knowledge of that. But if you would know of such an investigation or preparation for a prosecution, the Chamber would like to know from you. Are you aware of any such thing in other jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least now I have only had interviews with the Tribunal's investigators, but there has been no charges or accusations raised against me so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as far as you're aware of, no -- no specific investigations against you either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, finally I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that since you're testifying in open court, that whatever you say can be heard by the outside world, and I just want you to be aware of that. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know that, and there is nothing to hide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shala, you'll now be examined by Mr. Di Fazio, who's counsel for the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Shala, I wonder if you could just give us a few personal details. Firstly, your date of birth. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what your date of birth is, please.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It's the 17th of September, 1973.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't quite get the year he was born. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just speak up a little more clearly so that the interpreters in the booths can hear you and they'll interpret for me. Could you just repeat the year. They got the date and month -- the day and month but not the year. What year were you born?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: 1963. And that was in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Prizren in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were you educated in Kosovo? Did you go to school there?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. The primary school I carried out in Prizren, and my higher school in Boro i Ramiz in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. I want to ask you about events in 1998 in -- in Kosovo. And the first question I want to ask you about that particular time is whether you had any nicknames. Did you have any nicknames in -- in 1998?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. It was "The Wolf." My friends referred to me as "The Wolf."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: "The Wolf," and pronounced Ujku in Albanian; correct?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, in 1998, in the early part of 1998, did -- did you enter Kosovo from Albania?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember the date or -- or month? And if you can't remember that, if you can't remember the date or the month -- just hear -- wait for the question. If you can't remember the date or the month, can you remember what season it was?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. It was spring. After the killing of the Jasharis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember about how long after the killing of the Jasharis it was? Was it a matter of weeks or days? Months?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Two, three weeks, or a month. Many years have passed since. So I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fair enough. Can you tell the Trial Chamber about that crossing. How did you do it? Who were you with? And -- and what your purpose was.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: We got together a few friends. We met some other members who had worked as military officers. We met them together with Hasan Iliti [phoen]. We were living together in Tirana. And our aim was to go to Kosovo to protect the population so that the Jasharis case would not be repeated again. As far as we knew how to defend ourselves, we would do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And when you actually crossed over into Kosovo, about how many men were with you?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: 20, 30? Maybe 30. I don't know exactly. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And were you and these men carrying -- carrying cargo of any sort?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. We had our automatic weapons and munition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber about how much in the way of armaments and ammunition -- sorry, automatic weapons and ammunition you were -- each individual was carrying?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It was as -- as much as each one of us could carry. As much as we could carry, we got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And once across the mountains, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: We had someone who knew the way. He waited for us and led the way to Smonica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is that in a place -- in an area called Reka e Keqe?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you supposed to meet anyone there?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. We met Kenun [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And did you -- were you -- anyone else, or is that it?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: There were other people as well, but I can't remember their names. However, we didn't know each other's names. I don't even know them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the nickname Smajl?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In what context have you heard that nickname?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Smajl was supposed to come and meet us in Smonica, but at the time there were -- there was unrest in Decan and he couldn't come. No one could come from there. And it was the people from Smonica who -- who accompanied us up to the asphalted road, and then they told us up to -- to go up to Suka, the way up to Suka, and somebody else would come and meet us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. Thanks for that. Did you ever find out subsequently who Smajl was?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes, later on. Late. After I stayed in Gllogjan for a while, and then I knew who Smajli was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you find -- or who did you discover Smajli or Smajl to be?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: He was the father of Nasim and the father of Agron. Smajl Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what was his first name?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Smajl.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he have any other names apart from Smajl?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It was Smajl Haradinaj. He was the father of Nasim and Agron.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to play a portion of tape that -- of an interview that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I had understood that it wasn't Mr. Di Fazio's intention to examine the witness by reference to the transcripts of the interviews. Obviously the same conditions apply as with any other witness where the Prosecution seek to rely upon an earlier statement. In other words, once we get to the point where a memory refreshment circumstance arises, then in such a situation it is permissible for the Prosecution to seek recourse to earlier statements but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We do not know yet at this moment what Mr. Di Fazio wants, but perhaps -- perhaps you could explain, Mr. Di Fazio. Perhaps if you could take your earphones off for a while, Mr. Shala. Do you speak any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A little bit. [In English] A little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you're aware that the witness understands a little English? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Well, the portion of the interview I want to play is where this very topic was discussed as between investigators and the -- the witness. He offered information about the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that about what the first name was of the person he -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first perhaps try that in a different way. Before we play the video -- Mr. Shala, could you ... You were asked about the person with the nickname Smajl. I think you later said it was Smajl Haradinaj. Do you know what his official first name is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As -- as far as I know, it's the father of Nasim, and he is called Smajl Haradinaj. And we stayed in his place. We lived there. In -- in a Western country. But now I don't understand where the Prosecutor is going, but we -- we understand that Ramush also had his pseudonym as Smajl, but maybe I didn't understand the whole thing well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you say that apart from a father you just mentioned, that Ramush Haradinaj also was nicknamed Smajl? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I understood it. And Smajl Haradinaj, he was living in a Western country, and we weren't expecting an 80-year-old that Smajl Haradinaj was to come and meet us. So obviously it was Ramush who would come and meet us there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stress, Mr. Shala, that you have given a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth. That is that, if someone asks about persons by the nickname Smajl, that you mentioned everyone you know under that nickname, whether you consider it likely or not that it's relevant, but please tell us everything you know. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And thank you, Witness, for that clarification. All right. After you'd crossed the mountains and made your way to Smonica and -- in the area of Reka e Keqe, where did you ultimately end up, your -- your group of men?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: In Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was that very shortly after you crossed over the mountains? You -- a matter of a day or so?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It was a night or two. I don't know exactly which village it was. It was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreters have got a technical problem. Whenever I switch the mic, I can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have a technical problem with microphones at this moment. I don't know who's going to resolve it. Could I get a signal from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said that: "We passed the mountain. We spent one night in a village where we met someone who was cutting timber. And then we went to Jabllanice."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that then the technical problems have been resolved. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So you got to Jablanica. And where did you and the -- the group of men go? Where did you take up residence or ...?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: In the house of Lahi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think we've still got that problem. Whenever I switch the microphone on, I can't hear the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not your fault, Witness. There's a technical problem. Just wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shala, we have to take our time to see whether we can resolve it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Shall we have another go? I still can hear the echo, though. It's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shala, since the problem has not been resolved and since we are about to have a break anyhow, we'll take it a bit earlier. We will have a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Shala, just before the break you said that you got to Jablanica with your group of men and you took up residence in the house of Lahi. Lahi who?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever meet his -- let me rephrase that. Does he have a brother?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know what his name is?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: He was there. He came in later, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Nazmi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. And how long did you stay in Jablanica from that point onwards?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. Four weeks? Five? I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just trying to get a broad picture now. So you -- you go across the mountains, down to Jablanica. You're there for about four or five weeks. And after that, where -- where did you go?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Went to Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know of a place called Dujak?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever go there for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And about when was that in relation to your stay in Jablanica? Was it after the time -- after the four or five weeks had finished at Jablanica? Or did you go to Dujak and then return to -- to -- to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I went to Jabllanice first and then I went to Dujake, where I started work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So now let's focus on that period of time when you were in Jablanica before you went to Dujak. You've told us that you went to stay in the house of Lahi Brahimaj. Did you -- did you stay there throughout the time that you were in Jablanica, or did you move around?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: We didn't stay in one place. We -- we had lunch in one house, dinner in -- in another, because we couldn't be a burden to one single family all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And are you referring to that group of men that crossed the mountains with you?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you -- you know -- you've heard of the organisation the KLA.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Okay. Now, did it have a headquarters in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Headquarters? I don't know. That was a house where the superiors met. Just a house of Lahi. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fair enough. But when you say "the superiors," have you got any names or people in mind, or they were just superiors to you? Can you let us know?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I'm saying superiors, Gjelal Hajda was there. He slept there. I was living there. It was the so-called superiors, because all of us were soldiers, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And you -- when you say "superiors," you mean your superiors in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. And it was in Lahi's house that these superiors congregated from time to time. Is that -- is that --

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do I correctly understand you?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever attend such meetings?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. I was having my meals there. I was sleeping there. There was no formal meetings as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did you take orders from anyone?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: From the local headquarters commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Nazmi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about Lahi Brahimaj? Did he ever give you orders? Or can I ask you in addition to that: Were you aware of receiving orders that had emanated from him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what that last question means, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please reformulate the question. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Well, I'll take the easy way and split it into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about Lahi Brahimaj? Did he ever directly give you orders?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe. But I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in addition to the -- to the headquarters, was there a barracks anywhere in Jablanica? Or a building that served as a -- as a type of barracks?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And about how far from Lahi Brahimaj's house would that barracks have been?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It was at the entrance of the village; whereas, Lahi's house is in the heart of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I would like to show you a drawing. Yes, okay, you've told us at the entrance of the village, but about how far from the house would you say? Try and give us an idea in metres or kilometres.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't know the exact distance, because the village is not as big in terms of -- in terms of measuring it with kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Less than a kilometre?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I am not in a position even to -- to know how long a kilometre is. And I was only walking. I didn't use a car. I don't know how long the distance is, in terms of metres or kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I would like you -- I'm going to show you a diagram or a drawing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. You said you didn't use a car, you don't know how long a kilometre is. From the entrance of the village, how many minutes would it take you if you would walk there to the house of Lahi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five -- five, six minutes. Seven maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 2117.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, it's a -- a drawing or a plan that I want to show you here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need a number, Mr. -- MR. DI FAZIO: It will eventually, yes, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be number P1185.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we flip it -- oh, that's it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that your signature that you see at the top left-hand corner of that particular plan?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what does -- have a look at the plan. And perhaps we can flip it again so that it's on its side to make it easier for you. Okay. There we are. What -- and perhaps if we can make it a little bigger. That seems to be a diagram. Do you know what it represents?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber what -- what it -- what it's a plan of.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It's the barracks. There was a small house which was used as a barracks. And there was also a depot for the food --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: -- for the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that's the barracks that you just told His Honour it took about five or six minutes' walk from Lahi Brahimaj's house.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that's your drawing.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? No objection. Admitted into evidence, P1185. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And now while we've been talking about that particular diagram, Mr. Shala, I'd like to show you a photograph. Can the witness be shown D118. Thank you. Do you recognise that place, that -- that building, that area?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. But I haven't seen it in such a state. It's dilapidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's -- well, first questions first: Is that the barracks that you've just been talking about? And is that a photograph of the -- the buildings that you were trying to depict in that drawing I showed you just moments ago?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But when you last saw it, it was in better condition. And, what, were there more buildings or -- or was it just like that?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It was better. But I see the kitchen was destroyed, the place where bread was cooked was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Where did the soldiers -- let me rephrase that. You've described it as a barracks there. Did -- did soldiers actually sleep somewhere at that location?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes, in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the -- was there an office there?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes, there was a kind of office at the entrance, a so-called office, because only it had a desk inside and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. If I asked you to perhaps mark - if you -- if you can see it - the window or -- or part of the building that -- where this office was that you've just spoken about, could you do that, please? You see the pen can write on the surface of the screen. If you can just perhaps do an arrow pointing -- pointing -- perhaps an arrow.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps just put your initials underneath that, down at the bottom somewhere. On the screen.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that particular image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be number P1186.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I take it that there are no objections against it? Then it's admitted into evidence, P1186. MR. DI FAZIO: I still haven't finished with it, and so I'd like to save that image and have it as an exhibit, but I'd like the witness to be shown it again, please, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's still on the screen. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, I'm not sure of the technicalities of this. Do we not have to save this and show it again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if we save it, then, of course, no changes can be made any more. That's -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. MR. DI FAZIO: That would seem to be the safer course, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is it saved? It is. Please proceed. A number is already assigned. MR. DI FAZIO: Does that mean, Your Honours, that he can mark it again, if necessary? I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then, of course, it would need another number. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Got that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever go to this location in the weeks that you were at Jablanica before going to Dujak?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: About how often would you visit there? And for what reason?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: We went there to -- to have the meals, because the kitchen was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever go there for any other reason, or was it just to eat?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: To eat. But if I was riding in somebody's car, I would go there to get the petrol or diesel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And you can see the building on the -- on the right-hand side. It's obviously dilapidated there, and it's got a group of men standing out in front of it. What was that building on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It was the house where the soldiers slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Only soldiers in that house or -- or was it used for any other purpose?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I've seen soldiers only. I've seen nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Brahimaj? By that I mean Mr. Lahi Brahimaj or Mr. Nazmi Brahimaj in that place?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes, normally we -- we went there whenever we wanted to get soldiers from -- that's where we reported to get them. And, of course, the -- it was the village commander who decided who was going to go for a particular assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the time that you were in Jablanica before heading off to Dujak, did you ever meet a man named Miftar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I -- may I ask a question? Mr. Shala, you said it was the village commander who decided who was going to go for a particular assignment. Were you speaking of somebody in particular? Who was the village commander? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nazmi Brahimaj was the one who gave orders. And he had the list and he -- he decided who was going to go to collect weapons, who was going to go on a particular assignment. And I -- I got everything from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And is this the same as the village commander? Do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the village commander. He was the village commander. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know if Lahi Brahimaj ever gave orders to Nazmi Brahimaj or vice versa?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And now, I -- I -- unless I missed it, I didn't get an answer, I think, to my question, an earlier question. I asked you about a gentleman named Miftar. In the time you were in Jablanica, did you come to know a man named, or nicknamed, Miftar?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: There are many Miftars in the Albanian community, and I don't know about which person we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, think of it in this way: Does that mean that there were a lot of Miftars in Jablanica, or you met no one called Miftar in Jablanica, or you simply can't remember? Do your best and tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I can't remember, but in -- in every village there is a Miftar and I don't know about which Miftar we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to ask you about some other names. Alush Agushi, do you -- do you know him?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- now I know who that person is. Previously, I knew him by his alias. Now I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. And what was Alush Agushi's alias?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: We called him Pipi, because he had a problem with his throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see him in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was his relationship with Lahi Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I don't know this. I don't know their links.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Think back. Have you ever known what their relationship was? Have you ever been able to remember what their relationship was, if any?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I don't know. Whenever he came to Lahi's place, he was there among others. As to what relations they have, I don't know. They will properly know it. I don't know what relations and -- and how to understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me help you. Would you describe them as being very close? Not just professional acquaintances but actually close, good friends.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Arbnur Zeneli?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Excuse me. And did you ever see him in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've told us about the KLA and soldiers and so on. As far as you're aware, did the KLA ever develop, in whatever form - whatever form - a military police contingent in the area?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: No. We had the so-called military police, but it -- it was just to -- to check and make sure that the soldiers were ready, at hand to help out. But nobody had ever undergone any military police training as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thanks for that explanation. Were you a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I -- I had a black uniform of a so-called military policeman, but it was just a formal thing so that at least when people saw that kind of uniform that they could take us seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So I -- I gather from what you've just said that there was something called a military police entity but you didn't think much of it and you didn't think it was very organised or sophisticated. I don't want to put words in your mouth, but is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So let's call it the military police, whatever -- for the sake of being able to continue with this -- this questioning. And you can -- I'll give you an opportunity to describe it. Okay? You've said that you were in the -- in the military police. Do you -- who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I can't remember names, but we received an order in writing that for that period, for that period we would exercise the task of a military police. And -- and in this entity we could have the best capable people and that we would retrain people to do this task as best as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you know of -- or have you ever heard of a gentleman named Hasim Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Hasim?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Hasim Taqi or Thaqi. I apologise for my pronunciation. I think it's Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Sorry, are we talking about Hasim or Hashim?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll ask you another question and assist you. Have you ever heard of a man named "The Snake"?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know the Snake's real name or his proper name?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes, it's Hashim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did -- did he ever have anything to do with your appointment as a military police officer?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. But -- it's something I'm not sure about. Maybe yes; maybe no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you're unsure; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Would it help you if I played a tape that you gave -- a tape of an interview that you conducted with officers of the OTP two years ago? Would that help your -- would that assist your memory? I can do that.

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness -- I'd like --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'd like you to -- this tape -- you'll be able to see writing on the -- on the screen, and you'll be able to hear words as well. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as translation into English and French is concerned, the booth are aware that if it goes too quickly that -- MR. DI FAZIO: And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- one reads and follows whether the words written down are the spoken words and that the other interpreter then translates, even if a bit behind. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours please, if you -- I understand you've got binders. And you can find this in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the booth received any binders, Mr. Di Fazio? Yes, I see Ms. Gustafson is nodding "yes." MR. DI FAZIO: I believe so. I'm told that's covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And you'll find -- it's only a very small passage that I want to play. And it's tape 2742, B side, page 8, and it goes until page 10. All right? And so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You served as the head of the Military Police at the time? Sort of. Appointed. Who appointed you? The Snake. Dhjetshi. The Tenth. A nickname? The Ten, we knew him as the Ten. No, Hashim Thaqi was the Snake. Rexhep Selimi. It should be him. He was a short man. I don't follow -- I don't have a satellite box, and I don't follow much of the news so that I'd know where are they now or ... The Fifteenth. He was Lahi Brahimaj. MR. DI FAZIO: I want the next line. It's the very next line. Just the next line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You served as the head of the Military Police? Who appointed you? Dhjetshi. The Tenth. A nickname?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the question asked by Mr. Di Fazio, and as I understand it the purpose for which Mr. Shala was listening to the tape, he has received an answer. If he wishes to propose another question, perhaps that would be appropriate. Otherwise, he is at this point leading the witness in areas where we don't know where he's going. The specific question dealt with whether he'd been appointed and whether he knew Mr. Hashim Thaqi. We certainly have covered that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not entirely clear to me. Mr. Di Fazio, the questions were about Hashim Thaqi being the Snake. MR. DI FAZIO: And his -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who appointed the witness where he said he didn't remember. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The specific question was: Do you know the Snake's real name or his proper name? This is at page 39, line 10: "Yes, it's Hashim Thaqi. "Did he have anything to do with your appointment as a military police officer? "I don't know. I'm not sure." So we've got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get matters done in a more quick way. You have heard - and we could replay it - part of the interview you gave. We have on paper and up to what we heard the paper reflects what apparently is said on this statement. Now, let's just stick to the portion we just heard. You earlier said that you do not remember whether the Snake, or Hashim Thaqi, had anything to do with your appointment as a police officer. Mr. Di Fazio played this. Does that refresh your memory? Do you remember whether he was or was not involved in your appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my personal opinion that I was appointed by the persons who were present and the black uniform came from Drenica, because at that time we didn't have any uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you -- let me stop you there. Having heard the tape, and if the question is put to you again whether the Snake or, as he was called, Hashim Thaqi, did he have to do anything with your appointment as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have always believed so. I cannot be certain, however, because I didn't get any orders from him and I am not sure, but that's my personal belief. I thought he must have played a hand in my appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, was he the only one, or were there others who were involved in the appointment of you as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There have been others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you name them, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Tenth, the Fifteenth, because I knew them by numbers. It was much later that I learned their -- their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was the Fifteenth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lahi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lahi Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shala. I just want to show you another document now, and that will be 65 ter 2115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that need a number, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: It will eventually, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P1187.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Marked for identification. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I hope you can read that. Tell us if you can't. It's a bit small. The -- let's have a look at the top part of the document. Thank you, Mr. -- Mr. Registrar. This is a -- a document for the duties and rights of the military police or Policia Ushtarake, signed by a gentleman named Gjelal Hajda, Toni. Have you ever -- and there's also a signature on the document to the left. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: The one on the left side is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks for that. Have you seen that document -- sorry, let me be clearer. In 1998, did you ever see that document?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what about the man named Toni or Toni? Did you ever -- can you tell us who he is?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Gjelal Hajda.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks for that. We can read that. Was he known to you too? Was he operating in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes. We came together from Albania, and we stayed together until we went to Rahovec. I went there too for two days to help them. And from Rahovec I returned to Dujake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks for that. And underneath -- could we just slide the document down a bit and let's look at the other one, which we can see underneath that. That, I think I'm pretty confident, is the same -- essentially, the same content as the -- as the one above but signed by someone else. Firstly, is that your signature that you see on the left?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I don't think there's any dispute about that -- this, rather. That Nazmi Ibrahimaj's signature at the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If you can remember this, think back to this particular period of time. Do you know who actually gave you a copy of those military rules, those temporary internal regulations?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who was it who gave you those?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: It was -- the name of the person who gave it to me was Gjelal Ajdoni [as interpreted] and Nazmi Brahimaj, the commander of the local staff, and you have the signatures there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you remember approximately when you were given those documents because it's undated, so can you recall?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, but I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If I were to play to you the parts of the interview where you've commented on this, would it assist you memory? Would you like me to play the tape where you've commented on this, to help your memory?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes, you may. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. Well, let's just -- it's only a very short excerpt. I'd like to play to you this small passage. Your Honours will find this passage, if you just give me a moment, in 2742-B, page 11. Page 11.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, I have a document. These are -- the -- the upper part of the document concerns Rahovec and the lower part with the rules -- internal rules -- temporary internal rules for military police. This concerns Jablanica, and it's signed. It's signed by the commander of the local staff, Nazmi Brahimaj. There's no date? No, we didn't have any dates. Do you remember when he signed this? It could be two months after, one month after or one month and a half after we entered. So maybe somewhere in March? Latest April. But it shouldn't be May. Sorry, March -- end of March. And what exactly does the document say? Maybe you can translate it. It's the Rule of -- MR. DI FAZIO: We can stop it there, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm sorry. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Emmerson. I was looking at something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise. I wonder if the witness might remove his earphones. I appreciate that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second Mr. Shala.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm anxious to ensure that the proper foundation is laid and the proper use made of material if it's to be deployed as memory-refreshing material. Now, any of us who have studied these transcripts are aware that the witness has said, as he said in his evidence in chief, that he's entirely unaware of the date sequence but that, as he said in his evidence in chief a little while ago, he entered Kosovo sometime after the massacre of the Jasharis on the 5th of March. Now, because of the uncertainty that appears in this transcript about dates, a question is asked of him about when these documents were drafted, and he says one and a half to two months after I entered. And then a question is put to him on the basis of an misapprehension of his earlier answers, when it says: "So that would be sometime in March, would it?" Now, with the greatest respect, that is not a proper use of memory-refreshing material. On the contrary, it's memory-obfuscating material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I do understand the, well, we could say, criticism is that you seek to refresh the memory of the witness on the basis of an interview where he is confused as far as the chronology is concerned. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, he doesn't appear to be. He seems to have given it some thought and he -- he -- he's not emphatic about the actual period of time as well. There's some latitude in what he says. He says: "Could be two months. One month, or after one month and a half. So maybe somewhere in March." And he says: "At the latest April." And then he says: "But it shouldn't be May -- sorry, March, end of March." So I would accept that there's a lack of precision in -- in what he says, but he does give you some parameters. And obviously it must have happened after he crossed the mountains, and we know that that happened the Jashari family suffered their fate. So it's -- we know that it's sometime towards the end of May. But in the very answer, he's giving you -- he's not pretending to give you any sort of precision. He's only giving you a window, a period of time for the -- for the -- for the creation -- for the acceptance of this document. And the witness is -- in the interview is not pretending to do any more than that, and I'm not seeking to elicit anything -- evidence of anything more than his approximation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then would you please be very careful, because there's some merit in both in what you say, Mr. Emmerson, and in what you say, that is, that it might not be easy to reconcile all answers in their proper chronology and at the same time, as Mr. Di Fazio points out, the witness seems to have given it some thought about timing and --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. My concern, as Your Honours will have appreciated, is that he's given it some thought but he responds to a leading proposition - namely, March - put on the basis of inconsistent earlier answers and then from that extrapolates a date of one and a half to two months. Now, he said earlier in his interviews, as he said in his evidence in chief that, the starting date for entry postdates the entry into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Which, of course, postdates the Jashari massacre. Now, the reason I'm rising isn't because I can't understand the parameters that Mr. Di Fazio is seeking to identify. The reason I'm rising is because it is very important that if material is to be used genuinely on a memory-refreshing basis, then it must be material that can refresh a witness's memory, rather than simply a substitution of one memory for another. I don't -- I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This -- this becomes almost philosophical, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm laying down a marker at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The marker is there. Attention has been drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And it's -- you know, fundamentally the proposition that there shouldn't come a point - and I for my part would be alert, if I may, to raise objections if there does - when memory refreshing slips over into impeachment because it is the Prosecution who's chosen to elicit material on which they say they can properly rely from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The marker is there. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. Could you please put on your -- By the way, Mr. Di Fazio, a totally different question: I see on the list of the 13th of September, 0.5 hours. That's far beyond what you've used until now, isn't it? MR. DI FAZIO: It is. I've got to confess it is, if Your Honours please. And I'm aware of the consequences for us. I -- I must say that I'm making reasonably good progress. I know I've already -- that's a strange thing to say knowing that I've already exceeded the time limit, but I must ask for a little more time. I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you still need? MR. DI FAZIO: I -- could Your Honour just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I -- I'm forced to seek another 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 14 minutes? MR. DI FAZIO: 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 40. That brings us to more than triple what you asked for. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider it. Try to focus at this moment on the most important parts. We'll consider it during the first break. MR. DI FAZIO: I will. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm grateful to you to allow me -- to consider that, and I'll do my level best to move this -- to move this along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you should keep in your mind that it might be that you've got only time until the first break, which will -- we'll have at quarter past 5.00. MR. DI FAZIO: Quarter past. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know a -- a gentleman named Toger, or does the name Toger mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever meet such an individual in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And was he a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What position did he hold in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: He trained the -- the young soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What sort of soldiers? Regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: The voluntary soldiers. All of us were voluntary. We didn't have any regular army as such. We didn't have any proper institution to organise an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were there any units in -- operating in the area of Jablanica that were regarded as special units or any form of -- not part of the regular KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: In Jabllanice? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about other areas around Jablanica? For example, Rznic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would caution Mr. Di Fazio --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At a later phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- to be careful about leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio heard this admonition, more or less. Not to be understood in this way, Mr. Di Fazio. You understand I'm choosing the wrong word. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about Rznic? Perhaps I can -- I'll help you again. Did -- did -- did the man you knew as Toger, did you ever see him or know of him operating or being based somewhere other than Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I don't know. He had a base in Jabllanice. I know that he engaged in training young soldiers. But when Gllogjan was attacked, he remained in Gllogjan. And at a later phase he was appointed to operate as a commander of a special unit in Irzniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. It's that period of time that I'm interested in. Tell the Trial Chamber, if you can, about the special unit. Firstly, who -- who was responsible for creating this special unit?

utterances.speaker: PJETER SHALA
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that Togeri was the commander. As to who created that, I don't know. I know that Togeri trained the soldiers, that he was their commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You -- moments ago you said: "At a later phase he was appointed to operate as a commander of a special unit in Irzniq." So you know that he was appointed.
